meta.description: Technical case study of an academic dental-management application with Angular workflows and an interactive React and Three.js odontogram.

hero.title: DentalSys
hero.headline: A clinic workflow with an interactive 3D odontogram.
hero.intro: An academic dental-management project combining patient workflows, appointments, treatments and document handling with a separate interactive 3D odontogram.
hero.odontogramAlt: DentalSys interactive 3D odontogram showing synthetic dental states.

system.headline: A clinic-facing Angular shell.
system.body: The Angular application is the clinic-facing shell: patients, appointments, history, treatments and documents live in one interface. This was a functional academic build, not a production clinic system.
system.patientsAlt: DentalSys patient directory from a synthetic demo dataset, with workflow actions for history and treatments.

appointments.headline: Scheduling inside the same patient workflow.
appointments.body: Appointments are managed with FullCalendar and show distinct states. The calendar stays connected to the broader patient record instead of living as a separate tool.
appointments.calendarAlt: DentalSys month calendar showing synthetic appointments and status markers.

challenge.headline: Keep Angular for the clinic. Isolate the 3D frontend.
challenge.body: The distinctive problem was representing dental state interactively in 3D while the main clinic application stayed Angular. The odontogram was isolated as a separate Next.js, React and Three.js application. Angular embeds it through an iframe and passes the relevant identifier. The 3D frontend loads GLTF dental models and communicates through the same REST API contract.

treatment.headline: From a selected tooth to a treatment row.
treatment.body: A typical path is patient, odontogram, tooth state, then treatment. The screenshot shows synthetic treatments and is not a claim of clinical validation.
treatment.treatmentsAlt: DentalSys treatments dialog showing synthetic treatment rows over the patient list.

meta.title: Automation & QA | Raquel Terrazas
meta.description: Technical experience in web automation, data extraction, validation and QA using JavaScript, Node.js, Puppeteer and REST APIs.

hero.title: Automation & QA
hero.headline: Making web automation easier to trust.
hero.intro: Engineering and QA work around web automation, data extraction and validation — with an emphasis on debugging failures, checking outputs and making releases safer.
hero.context: Trilogy Software · Software Engineer — DAX · since October 2023

flow.visualAlt: Portfolio illustration of a web automation workflow: input, extract, normalize, validate, QA and release.

loop.headline: A simplified view of the engineering loop.
loop.frame: Not every task followed this exact sequence. It is a compact way to describe the work.

build.body: Automation work involves turning changing web interfaces and APIs into repeatable extraction workflows. The stack stays intentionally small: JavaScript, Node.js, Puppeteer and REST APIs.

validate.headline: A successful run is not the same as a correct result.
validate.body: QA here is more than asking whether a script finished. The useful question is whether the output is shaped correctly, complete enough, and still trustworthy after a change.

layers.structureBody: Is the output shaped correctly? Example: records is an array.
layers.contentBody: Are expected fields present and plausible? Example: price is a number.
layers.regressionBody: Did a change break previously working behavior?
layers.releaseBody: Is the result ready for final validation and deployment?

debug.body: When a run fails, the useful artifact is a short, readable trace: what was expected, what arrived, and which check broke. The card on the right is an original, simplified example — not employer output.
debug.label: Illustrative debug trace

tooling.body: The same practice included small tools and scripts that made QA and repetitive validation easier to repeat. Those helpers stay unnamed here; they were internal, not an open-source product.

lifecycle.body: The work moved across implementation and quality, not only one isolated script.

principles.failBody: A silent wrong result is often worse than a visible failure.
principles.outputsBody: A successful run does not guarantee correct data.
principles.changeBody: Web interfaces evolve; automation needs clear failure points.
principles.debugBody: Useful context and repeatable checks reduce investigation time.

reflection.body: Automation taught me that reliability is not just making software run; it is making failures understandable and results verifiable.
